[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Geometric Transformations and Interpolation in Computer Vision"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Geometric transformations are fundamental operations in computer vision that alter the spatial arrangement of pixels in an image. Common transformations include translation, rotation, scaling, shearing, and affine or perspective projections. These transformations are widely used in image registration, augmented reality, rectification, and deep learning data augmentation."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Mathematical Foundation of Affine Transformations"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An affine transformation preserves lines and parallelism, though not necessarily lengths and angles. It can be represented in homogeneous coordinates by a 3x3 matrix multiplication combining linear transformations (rotation, scaling, shear) and translation."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import cv2
import numpy as np

# Load an image
image = cv2.imread('input.jpg')
rows, cols, _ = image.shape

# Define source and destination points for affine transformation
pts1 = np.float32([[50, 50], [200, 50], [50, 200]])
pts2 = np.float32([[10, 100], [200, 50], [100, 250]])

# Get the affine transformation matrix
M = cv2.getAffineTransform(pts1, pts2)

# Apply the affine transformation
dst = cv2.warpAffine(image, M, (cols, rows))"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"The Role of Interpolation"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"When an image undergoes geometric transformation, output pixel locations often fall in between input pixel coordinates (sub-pixel locations). Because images are discrete grids, interpolation is required to estimate pixel intensity values at these new coordinates."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Nearest Neighbor Interpolation: Assigns the value of the closest pixel. Fast, but produces blocky artifacts and stair-stepping."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Bilinear Interpolation: Uses the weighted average of the 4 nearest pixels. Smooths results better than nearest neighbor with minimal computational overhead."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Bicubic Interpolation: Considers the 16 nearest pixels. Produces much smoother results and sharper edges, though computationally more expensive."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Interpolation with OpenCV"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"# Resizing an image using Bicubic Interpolation
height, width = image.shape[:2]
scaled_image = cv2.resize(image, (width * 2, height * 2), interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Backward Mapping and Aliasing"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"To prevent holes (undefined pixels) in the output image, transformation engines typically use backward mapping (inverse mapping). Instead of mapping pixels from the source to the destination, algorithms iterate over every destination pixel and compute its corresponding location in the source image, applying interpolation to fetch the intensity."}]
